content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on improving the visual interpretability of the CLIP model with architectural design. It considers visual grounding capability as interpretability, and proposes to address the issues by switching the model backbone and adding additional pooling/attention layers. Experimental results show that the method is able to achieve improvements on two evaluation metrics defined in the paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
As far as I am concerned, this paper has the following strengths:

(1) Interpretability is an essential component for AI systems applicable to real-world scenarios, and yet less studied in the field of large-scale pretraining.

(2) The paper carries out extensive analysis to locate the issues, and provides a potential solution that shows certain improvements.

However, there are also some notable weaknesses:

(1) I am not surprised that CLIP does not have good visual interpretability. Contrastive learning in the original model is performed only between the class token (i.e., [CLS]) of the visual encoder and text, and there is no explicit support for the alignment of visual tokens and text. I believe forcing interpretability on visual tokens is not an ideal choice for CLIP. There is a recent paper [ref1] that tackles a similar problem (i.e., lack of visual grounding capability) but with a different learning paradigm.

(2) While the emphasis of the paper is on contrastive learning, the proposed masked max pooling essentially changes the original CLIP visual encoder with the self-supervised DINO. This is counterintuitive and somewhat contradictory to me. Why should we solve problems of contrastive learning by switching to another type of method? 

(3) The motivations behind the newly introduced evaluation metrics are unclear. The proposed mMIoU is basically a special form of IoU, and the requirement on grid search makes the evaluation sensitive to statistics of specific datasets. Additionally, I am not fully convinced why we should use visual grounding (i.e., mFMB) to estimate recognition performance.

(4) The paper limits its scope to visual grounding in the zero-shot image recognition task, while a key strength of CLIP is its generalizability to various vision-and-language applications. To better understand the interpretability of contrastive learning, a broader set of tasks need to be considered.

(5)  Most performance gain in recognition comes from the substitution of the backbone (from contrastive learning to self-supervised learning, Table 3). As mentioned in the above comment, the original CLIP does not have good support for visual grounding, and thus inferior interpretability scores are expected. For a more thorough estimation of the accuracy and interpretability of contrastive learning, I would suggest that the authors consider comparing with [ref1].

[ref1] RegionCLIP: Region-based Language-Image Pretraining. CVPR, 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
(1) The proposed ITSM essentially measures the cosine similarity between visual and text tokens, which is commonly used for estimating alignment between modalities.

(2)  The dual projection is about combining predictions from the class token and the visual tokens with two sets of layers, which are of relatively incremental technical contributions.

(3) The presentation of the paper can be improved. There is no “Related Works” section in the main paper, which makes it difficult for some readers to understand the background. 

(4) No code is provided for reproducing the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper highlights an important problem in large-scale pretraining, I am not fully convinced about the proposed methods, largely because of the choices of methods for tackling the issues (e.g., switching backbone, focusing on visual tokens which are not naturally supported for the task) and the lack of motivations. I also have some concerns about the limited scope and novelty of the paper. Therefore, I am leaning towards rejecting it.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper visualizes vision features learned by CLIP and observes that CLIP prefers background regions over foreground regions. The authors further dive deep into this issue and find that the root cause is the pooling part. Therefore, they propose a new pooling method named Masked Max Pooling with attention from the image encoder to encourage improved visual interpretability. They also propose dual projections to ensure that the recognition accuracy won’t drop significantly.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The investigation of CLIP’s visual interpretability is new and the observations are interesting.
2. Detailed analyses are provided in this work.

Weakness:

Major comments:
1. To verify that the new pooling method cannot degrade the recognition accuracy, this paper only uses multi-label recognition tasks. Why not also verify it on other tasks, such as ImageNet classification and retrieval? (Note: this comment is not requesting new experiments)
2. The writing is not clear, which makes it hard to understand (see moderate comments below).
3. The contribution of this paper is marginal. Although we care about the visual interpretability, we cannot sacrifice the model performance.
4. To my understanding, the “erroneous visualization” is not introduced by CLIP’s contrastive training. Instead, this is an inherent property of ViT.

Moderate comments: 
1. This paper always uses something like $X \in R^{a, b}$ to represent a matrix/tensor. It is better to use $X \in R^{a \times b}$.
2. In Equation 3, it is not suggested to use “X” to represent matrix/tensor multiplication.
3. In Equation 4, how was “reshape” and “resize” implemented? More details are required to help readers to understand.
4. In Equation 5, what is $M_r$?
5. Equation 6 is not clear. What is “s” and what does classification represent here? Shouldn’t “X:1,:” be a class token? Why is it called the first image token?
6. A grid search (step 0.01) is performed to find the foreground threshold. Is that performed for each evaluation task? How to determine this threshold?
7. In Equation 7, add a space between $s.t.$ and $i$
8. How GMP is performed on image features?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity needs to be improved significantly. Although improving CLIP’s visual interpretability is novel, the contribution and quality of this paper is limited. Since a lot of technical details are missed, it is hard to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: The investigation of CLIP’s visual interpretability is interesting, but the contribution of this paper is very limited. Given that a lot of details are not clarified, I vote to reject this work.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper explores the visual interpretability of a state-of-the-art visual-language model: CLIP. The authors first propose the image-text similarity map (ITSM) technique, and find that this ITSM technique shows visual attention maps which indicate the CLIP model learns to focus on the background rather than the foreground. Based on experiments by trying out different pooling operations (e.g. average pooling and max pooling), the authors find empirically that the reason of false visual explanations is caused by the pooling part, because an average pooling operation can cause the feature to shift in semantics and make the text features falsely aligned to the background.

To address the problem of the first proposed ITSM technique, the authors propose a "masked max pooling" operation which uses self-attention maps from the image encoder to replace the pooling operation. With this new attention-based pooling operation, the authors show better interpretable attention maps for CLIP.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The paper studies an interesting research topic, i.e., explain the features of the CLIP model.

+ The authors discover an interesting problem, i.e., average pooling operation can cause semantic shift and propose a reasonable solution to address this problem.

- The formulation of "image-text similarity map" (ITSM) in Section 2.1 for CLIP seems wrong for the vision transformer. The authors claim that the ITSM technique proposed for CLIP is similar to the class activation map (CAM) proposed for standard CNN. However, while a CNN can preserve the spatial location in feature maps with locality, the vision transformer in CLIP does not have the inductive bias to encode spatial information in the same way as CNN (see [a]). This is because in vision transformer, the features have gone through global self-attention, and therefore a feature vector is not guaranteed to map to a spatial location in image. 

- There should be more comparison to existing visual explanation methods, especially the ones used for vision transformer. Because the image encoder used in CLIP for experiments in this paper is ViT, it is necessary to compare to existing representative methods such as attention roll-out [b], and [c], [d].

- There should be more experiments to evaluation the model design with more metrics such as the perturbation test in [c] to quantitatively evaluate the quality of the produced attention maps. 

- It would be interesting to discuss the difference between the proposed method and the multi-modal neuron [e] which is another way to interpret the CLIP model. 

[a] An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale, ICLR 2020
[b] Quantifying attention flow in transformers. arXiv 2020
[c] Transformer Interpretability Beyond Attention Visualization. CVPR2021
[d] Generic Attention-model Explainability for Interpreting Bi-Modal and Encoder-Decoder Transformers. ICCV2021 
[e] Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks. 2021, https://distill.pub/2021/multimodal-neurons/
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
Most parts of the paper are overall clearly written. However, some parts need more efforts to improve the clarity. For instance, the Section 2.1 needs more explanations and details about the propose techniques and the formulas, e.g., what each notation means. 

Quality: 
1) The proposed method needs more clarification as the formulation seems ill-posed for vision transformer in CLIP. 
2) The experiments needs more comparison to the state-of-the-art methods as detailed in the strength and weakness section.

Novelty: 
The authors claim that it is a prior work to interpret CLIP from feature map, however, there is exiting works that study interpretability of visual language models such as [d,e]. It would be important to compare and discuss these existing works.

Reproducibility:
There is no code available currently. It is recommended to release the code if published.

[d] Generic Attention-model Explainability for Interpreting Bi-Modal and Encoder-Decoder Transformers. ICCV2021 
[e] Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks. 2021, https://distill.pub/2021/multimodal-neurons/
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper needs more efforts in improving the design of the method, including comparison to more related methods [b,c,d], and using relevant metrics (e.g. perturbation test) as suggested in the strength and weakness section. 

[b] Quantifying attention flow in transformers. arXiv 2020
[c] Transformer Interpretability Beyond Attention Visualization. CVPR2021
[d] Generic Attention-model Explainability for Interpreting Bi-Modal and Encoder-Decoder Transformers. ICCV2021
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper starts by pointing out how CLIP focuses on the backgrounds of the image when visualized with its spatial feature magnitude. The phenomenon was obvious regardless of using attention visualization, similarity heatmap, and GradCAM. The authors investigated the cause and found that the average pooling of the image features is the main cause that made foreground features move to the background (dubbed as feature shift in the paper). Since max pooling was free from moving features' spatial position, the authors resorted to adopting max pooling to aggregate image features. The authors measured the interpretability using two new metrics they suggested (mMIoU and mFMB), which went up by adopting the max pooling. To compensate for decreasing classification accuracy, they re-trained CLIP with the CC3M dataset with LIT trick using DINO pre-trained weight.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- (C1) DINO [1] is well-known for its localization capability. As the authors constantly mentioned that the localization improvement of the ICLIP is partly due to "self-supervised" image encoders, I am curious if the statement holds for other SSL pre-trained + LIT-trained CLIPs. I suspect masked image modeling methods (SimMIM [2], MAE [3], BEiT [4]), contrastive learning methods (SimCLR [5], MoCo [6]), clustering (DeepCluster [7, 8], SwAV [9]), and bootstrapping (BYOL [10], DINO) all represent different localization performances.
- (C2) To separate the effect of the proposed methods, I think one more row is needed for Table 3, which is basic CLIP + masked max pooling (not basic CLIP + SSL-LIT + masked max pooling).
- (C3) I strongly recommend reporting the Imagenet-1K zero-shot classification accuracy, as we can still reasonably compare the performance for that metric on a low-data regime by referencing the OpenCLIP [11] repository's reports.
- (C4) What was the monitor metric the authors used for the grid search of the foreground threshold?
- (C5) In the introduction, the authors mentioned that this phenomenon is opposed to the behaviors of single modality models. However, the background shortcut is a well-known bias of classification-trained single-modality models [12].
- (C6) In section 2.1 and throughout the paper, the authors spared a lot of surface for the equations. However, I failed to find a detailed explanation of how the "pooling" is performed. Following equation 3, the manuscript clearly denotes that ITSM M has a dimension of H x W x N_t. So I first thought that the pooling is used to reduce N_t to a scalar value because that is the only way to display ITSM with the heatmaps in figure 2. However, following figure 4, it seems N_t is already reduced in the text encoder, which makes ITSM M have a dimension of H x W. Please address the mismatched equations and figures.
- (C7)
  - Typo: (page 3) Match Inter of Union → Match Intersection of Union
  - Typo: (page 6) Eg.1 → Eq.1
  - Typo:  (page 7) "the difference compared with CLIP is the image, encoder" → "the difference compared with CLIP is the image encoder"
  - Typo:  (page 8) 32.85%, 16.35%, 49.10%, 43.96% improvements → 32.85%p, 16.35%p, 49.10%p, 43.96%p


[1] Caron, Mathilde, et al. "Emerging properties in self-supervised vision transformers." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision*. 2021.
[2] Xie, Zhenda, et al. "Simmim: A simple framework for masked image modeling." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition*. 2022.
[3] He, Kaiming, et al. "Masked autoencoders are scalable vision learners." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition*. 2022.
[4] Bao, Hangbo, et al. "BEiT: BERT Pre-Training of Image Transformers." *International Conference on Learning Representations*. 2021.
[5] Xie, Zhenda, et al. "Simmim: A simple framework for masked image modeling." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition*. 2022.
[6] He, Kaiming, et al. "Momentum contrast for unsupervised visual representation learning." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition*. 2020.
[7] Caron, Mathilde, et al. "Unsupervised pre-training of image features on non-curated data." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision*. 2019.
[8] Caron, Mathilde, et al. "Deep clustering for unsupervised learning of visual features." *Proceedings of the European conference on computer vision (ECCV)*. 2018.
[9] Caron, Mathilde, et al. "Unsupervised learning of visual features by contrasting cluster assignments." *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 33 (2020): 9912-9924.
[10] Grill, Jean-Bastien, et al. "Bootstrap your own latent-a new approach to self-supervised learning." *Advances in neural information processing systems* 33 (2020): 21271-21284.
[11] [https://github.com/mlfoundations/open_clip](https://github.com/mlfoundations/open_clip) [12] Geirhos, Robert, et al. "ImageNet-trained CNNs are biased towards texture; increasing shape bias improves accuracy and robustness." *arXiv preprint arXiv:1811.12231* (2018).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- (Clarity) It was a bit difficult to understand the part of the paper due to mismatching equations and figures (see C6). In addition, there were parts that I had to read several times to understand what was being explained because attention map visualization and ITSM are being explained alternately. I believe this paper could be polished further.
- (Quality) This paper suggests using both self-supervised pre-trained image encoder + LiT and max pooling to boost the interpretability of the CLIP architecture. However, its impact on imagenet-1K zero-shot classification is unexplored (see C3) and its dependency on LiT is not addressed (see C2). Moreover, its claim of using SSL image encoder is too broad (see C1).
- (Novelty) The fact that this paper proposes new metrics to measure CLIP's interpretability and that it presents a model that actually performs well in those metrics can be considered novel.
- (Reproducibility) Source code is not provided, and no implementation details are provided. Since this work is an interpretability work, I believe it is essential to provide a working program that generates the heatmaps shown in the manuscript.
content.summary_of_the_review: It is difficult to give a high recommendation with the current submission. However, I would like to raise the score if my concerns are resolved.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The model proposed an improvement over the Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP), to make it attend to the most important regions (i.e. foreground) in the image. The paper proposed a method called masked max pooling. The mask is learned from a self-supervised image encoder. The paper proposed methods to quantitatively and qualitatively validate the claim that the new model brings more interpretability. They validate their model on VOC 2012 and MSCOCO 2017 dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
 - The paper is clear overall.
 - The idea is simple, but seems to be effective, with some caveat (mentioned below)
 - The proposed mFMB metrics can quantitatively evaluate the claim that the model brings more interpretability.

Weakness
- The major weakness is in experiments. I think the authors validate their claim with 3M data, but the mAP improvements (which is a standard metric) is still lower than the 400M data. Is there any way we can leverage datasets with larger sizes than 3M?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think the paper is very clear to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although there is a weakness as mentioned above, I think it is a minor one so I support acceptance, given its very good intuition and validations. Happy to adjust the score after rebuttal.
